```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false

library(tidyverse)
library(Rssa)
library(itsmr)
library(minpack.lm)
library(splines)
library(knitr)   # MASS is used via MASS::mvrnorm only, to avoid masking dplyr::select

## ---- analysis constants -------------------------------------------------
RECORD_START <- 1850      # ERSSTv6 begins January 1850; see Section 2.1
SPLIT_YEAR   <- 1938      # calendar split for the pre-industrial GAM training set
LOESS_SPAN   <- 0.25      # span of the non-harmonic smoother
GAM_K        <- 30        # GAM basis dimension
GAM_BS       <- "cc"      # cyclic cubic spline, as specified by the author
SST_SERIES   <- "anoma.mean"   # "anoma.mean" or "anoma.median"; see @sec-median

M.ssn <- c("season", 12, "season", 6)

## Rssa::parestimate returns a single "fdimpars.1d" object when `groups` has
## one element and a list of them otherwise.  Normalise to a list so the same
## extraction code works in both cases.
as_par_list <- function(pe) if (inherits(pe, "fdimpars.1d")) list(pe) else pe
esprit_period <- function(p) 1 / abs(unlist(p$frequencies)[1]) / 12   # years

## ---- data ---------------------------------------------------------------
## Updated NOAA ERSSTv6 global ocean series, re-extracted from the current grid
## by scripts/Ocean_mean.median_ts.R, joined to the SILSO-derived solar power
## variation from scripts/Sun_power.R.  Paths are located independently of where
## this document is rendered from.
find_project_file <- function(rel) {
  cands <- c(rel,
             file.path("..", rel),
             file.path("../..", rel),
             path.expand(file.path("~/projects/Ocean_Analysis", rel)))
  hit <- cands[file.exists(cands)]
  if (!length(hit)) {
    stop("Could not locate '", rel, "'. Working directory is '", getwd(),
         "'. Render this document from inside the Ocean_Analysis project.",
         call. = FALSE)
  }
  normalizePath(hit[1])
}

Ocean_NOAA.data <- readRDS(find_project_file("data/NOAA.OCEAN.ANOMALIES.rds"))
solar_mnthly    <- readRDS(find_project_file("data/S_power.rds")) %>%
  mutate(SI = TSI - mean(TSI))

noaa_source <- Ocean_NOAA.data$url.source
noaa_update <- Ocean_NOAA.data$update
raw_start   <- min(Ocean_NOAA.data$data$dt.mnth)
raw_n       <- nrow(Ocean_NOAA.data$data)
solar_to    <- max(solar_mnthly$dt.mnth)

## The SST grid may run a few months beyond the last SILSO month; the inner
## join keeps only months for which both are available.
oc <- Ocean_NOAA.data$data %>%
  dplyr::select(dt.mnth, Anomaly = all_of(SST_SERIES)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dt.mnth >= RECORD_START) %>%
  inner_join(dplyr::select(solar_mnthly, dt.mnth, Solar_Variation = SI),
             by = "dt.mnth") %>%
  arrange(dt.mnth) %>%
  mutate(anomaly = Resid(Anomaly, M.ssn))

N        <- nrow(oc)
time     <- oc$dt.mnth
rec_from <- min(time)
rec_to   <- max(time)
n_dropped <- raw_n - N
```

## Abstract {.unnumbered}

Attribution of long-term ocean warming requires that the secular anthropogenic component be separated from natural variability whose dominant periods — solar, bidecadal and interannual — are comparable in amplitude to the forced trend over multi-decadal windows. Here we decompose an area-weighted global ocean sea surface temperature (SST) anomaly record of `r N` monthly values (`r sprintf("%.2f", rec_from)`–`r sprintf("%.2f", rec_to)`) into (i) a *solar-locked* component, obtained by anchoring a cubic spline to the minima of a sunspot-derived solar-power proxy, (ii) an oscillatory field characterised by Singular Spectrum Analysis (SSA) with ESPRIT parameter estimation, and (iii) a secular industrial component defined as the residual against a Generalized Additive Model (GAM) baseline trained on the pre-`r SPLIT_YEAR` record and extrapolated forward.

```{r}
#| label: locked-trends
#| include: false

## nodes of the solar power variation (local minima of the irradiance anomaly)
stopifnot("Solar_Variation" %in% names(oc))
si <- oc$Solar_Variation
if (anyNA(si)) si <- zoo::na.approx(si, na.rm = FALSE) |> (\(v) ifelse(is.na(v), mean(v, na.rm = TRUE), v))()
find_nodes <- function(x) which(diff(sign(diff(x))) == 2) + 1
node_idx   <- find_nodes(si)
nodes_obs  <- time[node_idx]

cycle_gaps <- diff(nodes_obs)
mean_cycle <- mean(cycle_gaps)
sd_cycle   <- sd(cycle_gaps)
n_cycles   <- length(cycle_gaps)

## mean-cycle control: same number of knots, regular spacing at the mean period
nodes_mean <- seq(from = nodes_obs[1], by = mean_cycle, length.out = length(nodes_obs))
nodes_mean <- nodes_mean[nodes_mean > min(time) & nodes_mean < max(time)]
nodes_obs_in <- nodes_obs[nodes_obs > min(time) & nodes_obs < max(time)]

locked_trend <- function(knots) {
  fit <- lm(Anomaly ~ bs(dt.mnth, knots = knots, degree = 3), data = oc)
  as.numeric(predict(fit))
}

trend_phase <- locked_trend(nodes_obs_in)   # phase-locked (observed solar minima)
trend_meanc <- locked_trend(nodes_mean)     # mean-cycle control

## non-harmonic part of each locked trend
nonharm <- function(y) as.numeric(predict(loess(y ~ time, span = LOESS_SPAN, degree = 2)))

dat <- tibble(
  dt.mnth   = time,
  anomaly   = oc$anomaly,
  trd_phase = trend_phase,
  trd_meanc = trend_meanc
) %>%
  mutate(
    nh_phase  = nonharm(trd_phase),
    nh_meanc  = nonharm(trd_meanc),
    res_phase = anomaly - nh_phase,
    res_meanc = anomaly - nh_meanc,
    ## harmonic part of the locked trend, and the observed anomaly with that
    ## part removed -- the response of the growth-curve fit below
    har_phase = trd_phase - nh_phase,
    growth    = anomaly - har_phase
  )

## characteristic dates of the non-harmonic phase-locked trend
Min_early <- time[which.min(dat$nh_phase)]
branch1950 <- dat %>% dplyr::filter(dt.mnth > 1950) %>% pull(nh_phase)
Min_mid    <- 1950 + which.min(branch1950) / 12
branch1975 <- dat %>% dplyr::filter(dt.mnth > 1975) %>% pull(nh_phase)
Turn_late  <- 1975 + which.min(diff(branch1975)) / 12

rmse_constructions <- sqrt(mean((dat$nh_phase - dat$nh_meanc)^2))
```

ESPRIT identifies three regimes in the detrended field, listed in @tbl-esprit. The analysis is repeated with the spline knots placed at the **mean** sunspot-cycle interval of `r sprintf("%.2f", mean_cycle)` yr (standard deviation `r sprintf("%.2f", sd_cycle)` yr over `r n_cycles` cycles) rather than at the observed solar minima. That substitution is physically inferior — it discards the observed phase — and is used only as a null test: structure that survives regular knots cannot have been created by phase-accurate ones. The spread between the two constructions doubles as an empirical uncertainty scale for the estimated periods.

```{r}
#| label: industrial-fits
#| include: false

df_full  <- dat %>% dplyr::select(dt.mnth, anomaly, nh_phase, har_phase, growth)
df_train <- df_full %>% dplyr::filter(dt.mnth < SPLIT_YEAR)
n_train  <- nrow(df_train)

tt <- df_full$dt.mnth

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Growth-curve estimator, in two steps.
##   step 1  four-parameter logistic with a constant term, one nlsLM call
##   step 2  Richards, with the slope k held at the value returned by step 1,
##           so the secular rate is not re-estimated and the two curves differ
##           only in shape
## The response is the monthly series itself, NOT a low-pass filtered version
## of it: the filtered series is flat over long stretches, which is what makes
## the logit/asymptote search degenerate.  No staged asymptote separation and
## no starting-value search are needed -- nlsLM converges from the author's
## own starting values.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
fit_growth <- function(y, tt, start = list(b = -0.15, L = 0.80, k = 0.05, t0 = 1988)) {
  d <- tibble(tt = tt, y = y)
  fl <- try(nlsLM(y ~ b + L / (1 + exp(-k * (tt - t0))), data = d,
                  start = start, control = nls.lm.control(maxiter = 200)),
            silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(fl, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  cl <- coef(fl); k_fixed <- cl[["k"]]
  yl <- as.numeric(predict(fl))
  fr <- try(nlsLM(y ~ Lr + Delta / (1 + exp(-k_fixed * (tt - t0r)))^(1 / nu), data = d,
                  start = list(Lr = cl[["b"]], Delta = cl[["L"]], t0r = cl[["t0"]], nu = 1),
                  control = nls.lm.control(maxiter = 500)),
            silent = TRUE)
  if (inherits(fr, "try-error")) return(NULL)
  cr <- coef(fr); yr <- as.numeric(predict(fr))
  turn <- function(v) tt[which.max(diff(v)) + 1]
  list(logis = fl, rich = fr, y_log = yl, y_rich = yr,
       b = cl[["b"]], L = cl[["L"]], k = k_fixed, t0_log = cl[["t0"]],
       Lr = cr[["Lr"]], Delta = cr[["Delta"]], t0_rich = cr[["t0r"]], nu = cr[["nu"]],
       turn_log = turn(yl), turn_rich = turn(yr),
       infl_rich = cr[["t0r"]] - log(cr[["nu"]]) / k_fixed,
       lower = cl[["b"]], upper = cl[["b"]] + cl[["L"]],
       lower_r = cr[["Lr"]], upper_r = cr[["Lr"]] + cr[["Delta"]],
       reached = (tail(yl, 1) - cl[["b"]]) / cl[["L"]],
       rss_log = sum((y - yl)^2), rss_rich = sum((y - yr)^2),
       rmse_log = sqrt(mean((y - yl)^2)), rmse_rich = sqrt(mean((y - yr)^2)),
       se = tryCatch(summary(fl)$coefficients[, 2], error = function(e) rep(NA_real_, 4)))
}

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Route A -- solar-locked construction (primary).
## The harmonic part of the locked trend is removed from the observed monthly
## anomaly; what remains is the non-harmonic trend plus the retained monthly
## residual.  It carries the secular rise AND the observation noise, which is
## what keeps the non-linear fit well conditioned.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
fitA <- fit_growth(df_full$growth, tt)

## control: the same fit to the smooth non-harmonic trend alone.  If the two
## agree, the noise carried along in `growth` is doing no harm -- this is the
## "add white noise to the low-frequency series" check.
fitA_smooth <- fit_growth(df_full$nh_phase, tt)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Route B -- GAM baseline trained before SPLIT_YEAR and extrapolated.
## Kept as the alternative decomposition, fitted with the SAME estimator so
## that the comparison is of decompositions and not of fitting procedures.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
gam_train <- mgcv::gam(anomaly ~ s(dt.mnth, k = GAM_K, bs = GAM_BS), data = df_train)

df_results <- df_full %>%
  mutate(
    extrapol_pre      = as.numeric(predict(gam_train, newdata = df_full)),
    industrial_effect = anomaly - extrapol_pre,
    industr.smth      = hr(industrial_effect, N / 1:20)
  )

fitB <- fit_growth(df_results$industrial_effect, tt)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Headline quantities come from route A.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
growth_ok <- !is.null(fitA)

B_fixed   <- if (growth_ok) fitA$k        else NA_real_
t0_log    <- if (growth_ok) fitA$t0_log   else NA_real_
t_turn_log  <- if (growth_ok) fitA$turn_log  else NA_real_
t_turn_rich <- if (growth_ok) fitA$turn_rich else NA_real_
nu_hat      <- if (growth_ok) fitA$nu        else NA_real_
t0_rich     <- if (growth_ok) fitA$t0_rich   else NA_real_
t_infl_rich <- if (growth_ok) fitA$infl_rich else NA_real_
infl_shift  <- t_turn_rich - t_turn_log
analytic_gap <- t_infl_rich - t_turn_rich
lower_asymptote <- if (growth_ok) fitA$lower   else NA_real_
upper_asymptote <- if (growth_ok) fitA$upper   else NA_real_
lower_asymptote.rich <- if (growth_ok) fitA$lower_r else NA_real_
upper_asymptote.rich <- if (growth_ok) fitA$upper_r else NA_real_
span_reached <- if (growth_ok) fitA$reached else NA_real_

df_results$logist_fit <- if (growth_ok) fitA$y_log  else NA_real_
df_results$richardsB  <- if (growth_ok) fitA$y_rich else NA_real_

## model-free reading: steepest rise of the observed non-harmonic trend
t_turn_obs <- tt[which.max(diff(df_full$nh_phase)) + 1]

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Uncertainty of t0, from the non-linear fit, propagated by Monte Carlo.
## Model-conditional and assuming independent residuals, which the strongly
## autocorrelated monthly series violates -- a lower bound.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
set.seed(42)
ci_t0log <- c(NA_real_, NA_real_)
if (growth_ok) {
  V <- tryCatch(vcov(fitA$logis), error = function(e) NULL)
  if (!is.null(V)) {
    dr <- MASS::mvrnorm(20000, coef(fitA$logis), V)
    t0d <- dr[, "t0"]
    t0d <- t0d[is.finite(t0d)]
    if (length(t0d) > 100) ci_t0log <- unname(quantile(t0d, c(0.025, 0.975)))
  }
}
fmt_ci <- function(ci) if (any(is.na(ci))) "not available" else
  sprintf("%.1f - %.1f", ci[1], ci[2])

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## AIC.  Two comparisons, and they are not the same thing.
##  (i)  logistic vs Richards WITHIN a series: same response, directly
##       comparable.
##  (ii) route A vs route B: made comparable by scoring each route on the SAME
##       response -- the deseasonalised anomaly -- as
##          route A   anomaly_hat = harmonic part + growth curve
##          route B   anomaly_hat = GAM baseline  + growth curve
##       with the effective number of parameters of the smoothing step counted
##       in: the spline coefficients and the equivalent number of parameters of
##       the LOESS for route A, the GAM edf for route B.  The LOESS and GAM
##       degrees of freedom are effective, not exact, so differences of a few
##       AIC units should not be over-read.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
aic_from <- function(y, yhat, p) {
  n <- length(y); rss <- sum((y - yhat)^2)
  n * log(rss / n) + 2 * (p + 1)
}
p_spline <- length(coef(lm(Anomaly ~ bs(dt.mnth, knots = nodes_obs_in, degree = 3), data = oc)))
p_loess  <- tryCatch(loess(nh_phase ~ dt.mnth, data = dat, span = LOESS_SPAN, degree = 2)$enp,
                     error = function(e) NA_real_)
p_gam    <- sum(gam_train$edf)

aic_tbl <- tibble(
  Route = c("solar-locked", "solar-locked", "GAM baseline", "GAM baseline"),
  Growth = rep(c("logistic", "Richards (k fixed)"), 2),
  AIC_series = c(AIC(fitA$logis), AIC(fitA$rich), AIC(fitB$logis), AIC(fitB$rich)),
  AIC_anomaly = c(
    aic_from(df_full$anomaly, df_full$har_phase + fitA$y_log,  p_spline + p_loess + 4),
    aic_from(df_full$anomaly, df_full$har_phase + fitA$y_rich, p_spline + p_loess + 5),
    aic_from(df_full$anomaly, df_results$extrapol_pre + fitB$y_log,  p_gam + 4),
    aic_from(df_full$anomaly, df_results$extrapol_pre + fitB$y_rich, p_gam + 5)),
  k  = c(fitA$k, fitA$k, fitB$k, fitB$k),
  t0 = c(fitA$t0_log, fitA$t0_rich, fitB$t0_log, fitB$t0_rich),
  nu = c(NA, fitA$nu, NA, fitB$nu),
  turn = c(fitA$turn_log, fitA$turn_rich, fitB$turn_log, fitB$turn_rich),
  ceiling = c(fitA$upper, fitA$upper_r, fitB$upper, fitB$upper_r),
  reached = c(fitA$reached, fitA$reached, fitB$reached, fitB$reached)
) %>% mutate(dAIC_anomaly = AIC_anomaly - min(AIC_anomaly))

aic_best_route <- aic_tbl$Route[which.min(aic_tbl$AIC_anomaly)]
aic_best_growth <- aic_tbl$Growth[which.min(aic_tbl$AIC_anomaly)]
dAIC_richards_A <- AIC(fitA$rich) - AIC(fitA$logis)

## agreement between the noisy and the smooth response (white-noise control)
noise_shift_t0 <- fitA$t0_log - fitA_smooth$t0_log
noise_shift_k  <- fitA$k      - fitA_smooth$k

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Narrative fragments
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
say <- function(x, fmt = "%.1f") if (growth_ok && is.finite(x)) sprintf(fmt, x) else "not identified"

growth_abstract <- sprintf(paste0(
  "Fitted in two steps -- a four-parameter logistic to fix the secular rate, then a Richards curve with that ",
  "rate held fixed -- the symmetric logistic turns in %.1f and the asymmetric curve, with shape $\\nu = %.3f$, ",
  "turns in %.1f, a shift of %+.1f yr. The record reaches only %.0f%% of the fitted span, so the upper ",
  "asymptote of %.2f degrees C is an extrapolation and not an estimate."),
  t_turn_log, nu_hat, t_turn_rich, infl_shift, 100 * span_reached, upper_asymptote.rich)

growth_discussion <- sprintf(paste0(
  "With the fitted $\\nu = %.3f$ and slope $B = %.4f$ yr$^{-1}$, the asymmetric curve turns at %.1f against ",
  "%.1f for the symmetric one, a shift of %+.1f yr. Read from the analytic root $t_0 - \\ln\\nu/B$ the same date ",
  "is %.1f, so the discrete and continuous readings agree to %.2f yr -- well inside the monthly sampling ",
  "interval, which is the resolution the data actually carry. Repeating the fit on the smoothed non-harmonic ",
  "trend alone, without the retained monthly residual, moves $t_0$ by %.2f yr and $k$ by %.4f yr$^{-1}$: the ",
  "noise carried along in the response changes nothing in the estimates and keeps the optimisation well ",
  "conditioned."),
  nu_hat, B_fixed, t_turn_rich, t_turn_log, infl_shift, t_infl_rich, abs(analytic_gap),
  noise_shift_t0, noise_shift_k)

growth_conclusion <- sprintf(paste0(
  "a signal near zero before the Second World War that turns at %.1f under the symmetric form and %.1f once the ",
  "upper-limb curvature $\\nu = %.3f$ is released, on a trajectory towards an asymptote of %.2f degrees C that ",
  "the record does not reach -- only %.0f%% of the fitted span lies inside the observation window"),
  t_turn_log, t_turn_rich, nu_hat, upper_asymptote.rich, 100 * span_reached)

df_final <- df_results %>%
  dplyr::select(dt.mnth, anomaly, "indus.trend" = richardsB,
                "pre_ind" = extrapol_pre, industrial_effect) %>%
  mutate(growth = df_full$growth, nh_phase = df_full$nh_phase)
```

The industrial residual is near zero before the Second World War and accelerates after 1950. `r growth_abstract`

Superposition of the isolated components shows that multi-decadal natural minima near `r sprintf("%.0f", Min_early)` and around the turn of the century oppose the industrial trend. The moderated slope of the raw anomaly record in the late twentieth century is therefore reproduced here as destructive interference between a deepening natural trough and a steepening forced trend rather than as a slowdown in forcing. Because the natural baseline is obtained by extrapolation, the magnitude of this effect is model-dependent; Section 5.4 states the sensitivities that bound the result.

## Plain Language Summary {.unnumbered}

The ocean surface has warmed since the nineteenth century, but the warming has not been steady. Natural rhythms — most of them tied to the roughly eleven-year and twenty-year solar cycles and to the Pacific — push ocean temperature up and down by a few tenths of a degree over decades, and these swings sit on top of the warming caused by industrial emissions. This study separates the two. We first build a curve that follows the natural solar rhythm, then use signal-processing methods to measure the length and stability of each natural cycle, and finally estimate what the ocean would have done without industrial influence by projecting forward a statistical model fitted only to data before `r SPLIT_YEAR`. The difference between the observed record and that projection is our estimate of the industrial effect. To check that the solar rhythms we find are really in the ocean data and not merely a consequence of how we built the curve, the whole analysis is repeated with the curve tied to a regular, average-length solar cycle instead of the observed one. The result suggests that a natural cold phase around the turn of the century partly hid the human-caused warming of the late twentieth century, so the underlying forced trend over that period was steeper than the raw record suggests. How much steeper depends on assumptions in the projection, which we state and test.

# Introduction

## Motivation

Global ocean heat content is the principal reservoir of the planetary energy imbalance, and SST is its most densely observed expression. Because roughly ninety per cent of the incoming solar energy retained by the climate system is stored in the ocean, the ocean surface record carries both the secular signature of anthropogenic forcing and the imprint of natural variability in the incident and absorbed solar flux. Separating the two is the classical attribution problem in its most direct form.

The difficulty is one of timescale overlap rather than of amplitude. Over a window of two to three decades, the amplitude of multi-decadal natural variability in SST is of the same order as the accumulated forced trend. Trends estimated over such windows therefore inherit the phase of the natural cycles at their endpoints, which is the mechanism behind the widely discussed moderation of surface warming in the 1998–2013 period (Kosaka and Xie 2013; Medhaug et al. 2017).

## Previous approaches

Two families of method dominate. The first removes known modes of variability by multiple regression on indices of the El Niño–Southern Oscillation, volcanic aerosol loading and total solar irradiance, and interprets the residual as the forced signal (Foster and Rahmstorf 2011). This is transparent but presupposes that each index is an adequate and mutually independent predictor, and that the response is instantaneous and linear. The second family is data-adaptive: Singular Spectrum Analysis and related subspace techniques extract oscillatory components from the record itself without prescribing their form (Golyandina et al. 2001; Golyandina and Korobeynikov 2014), at the cost of requiring a separate criterion to decide which reconstructed components constitute "trend" and which "variability".

## Aim and structure of this study

This study combines a physically anchored construction of the natural component with a data-adaptive characterisation of it. Specifically we ask:

1.  Can a trend anchored to the phase of the solar power variation (the *solar-locked trend*) isolate the harmonic content of the SST record more cleanly than a purely statistical smoother?
2.  What are the periods, damping rates and stationarity of the resulting oscillatory modes, estimated objectively rather than assumed — and how much of that structure is imposed by the anchoring itself?
3.  If the pre-`r SPLIT_YEAR` record is taken as an approximation of the pre-industrial state, what secular component does the later record require, and what functional form does it take?
4.  How do the isolated natural and industrial components interfere, and what does that interference imply for trends estimated over short windows?

Section 2 describes the data, Section 3 the methods, Section 4 the step-by-step results, and Section 5 the interpretation and the limitations that bound it.

# Data

## Sea surface temperature anomalies

Monthly SST fields are taken from the NOAA Extended Reconstructed Sea Surface Temperature, version 6 (ERSSTv6; `sst.mnmean`), as distributed by NOAA PSL (Huang et al. 2025). ERSSTv6 replaces the EOT reconstruction of version 5 by the AAN method and revises the quality control; its monthly fields begin in January 1850, four years earlier than version 5. The land–ocean classification and the ocean fraction of each grid cell are taken from the Berkeley Earth land/ocean product (Rohde and Hausfather 2020); grid cells with a land fraction above 10 per cent are excluded.

A global mean is formed as a double-weighted average: each cell is weighted by its ocean fraction and by its area relative to an equatorial cell, so that the result is an area-true ocean-only mean rather than a grid-cell mean. Both the weighted mean and the weighted median were computed; the mean is used throughout, with the median retained as a robustness check against localised outliers.

The analysis uses the full record: `r N` monthly values covering `r sprintf("%.2f", rec_from)`–`r sprintf("%.2f", rec_to)`, with no leading segment discarded. The global ocean mean was re-extracted from the current ERSSTv6 grid (`r raw_n` monthly fields, downloaded `r noaa_update`). The analysis window ends at `r sprintf("%.2f", rec_to)` because the sunspot record used for the solar proxy currently ends at `r sprintf("%.2f", solar_to)`; the `r n_dropped` SST months beyond that are held back by the join until the SILSO download is refreshed.

## Solar proxy

Daily international sunspot numbers (version 2.0) are obtained from WDC-SILSO, Royal Observatory of Belgium, and aggregated to monthly means. Total solar irradiance is then computed from the sunspot number using a published second-degree polynomial calibrated against top-of-atmosphere irradiance measurements, and only the anomaly about its long-term mean is retained. The zero crossings of that anomaly are physical events — the transitions of the solar forcing about its mean level — and it is those, not a nominal cycle length, that define the spline knots in Section 3.1. The intervals between them vary from `r sprintf("%.1f", min(cycle_gaps))` to `r sprintf("%.1f", max(cycle_gaps))` yr (@tbl-cycles), and that irregularity is a property of the forcing rather than noise in it: the series is treated throughout as irregularly spaced in solar phase, which is also why a subspace method such as SSA, which makes no assumption of a fixed period, is used to characterise the oscillatory field.

## Pre-processing

The annual and semi-annual cycles — the latter dominant at the equator — are removed from the anomaly series using the classical seasonal-means estimator of the `itsmr` package with harmonics at 12 and 6 months. All subsequent analysis operates on this deseasonalised series.

# Methods

## Construction of the solar-locked trend

The variable solar power passes through a minimum once per Schwabe cycle. The times of these minima define a set of knots that is fixed by solar phase alone and is not derived from the SST record. A cubic B-spline basis with knots at those times is regressed on the deseasonalised SST anomaly, giving the *solar-locked trend*: a curve free to follow the ocean record, but whose flexibility is licensed only at solar-phase transitions.

This construction is the methodological core of the study, and the reason for it is a specific one. A conventional smoother places its degrees of freedom by a bandwidth, a window length or a training span — quantities that belong to the analysis rather than to the ocean, and whose values then propagate into every result. A decomposition whose answer changes when the record is extended by a decade, or when a split year is moved, is reporting its own parameters. Anchoring the knots to the solar minima removes that class of dependence at the source: the knot positions are fixed by the Sun, the number of knots follows from the length of the record rather than being chosen, and no window, span or split enters the construction. @sec-window tests whether the freedom actually obtains.

## The mean-cycle control {#sec-meancycle}

Anchoring knots to solar minima and then reporting solar periodicities in the residual field is open to the objection that the periodicity is partly imposed by the construction. To bound that effect, the entire trend construction is repeated with the knots placed at a **constant** interval equal to the mean observed cycle length,

$$\bar{T} = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^{n}\bigl(\tau_{i+1}-\tau_i\bigr) = `r sprintf("%.2f", mean_cycle)`\ \text{yr},$$

where $\tau_i$ are the observed solar minima, starting from the first observed minimum and using the same number of knots. The mean-cycle series carries the same number of degrees of freedom and the same average spacing as the phase-locked series, but no information about the actual timing of individual cycles.

The control is a null test, not an alternative analysis. Replacing the observed crossings by a regular sequence deliberately introduces a phase error that grows with distance from the anchor, so the mean-interval construction is physically inferior to the phase-locked one and is never used downstream. Its single purpose is falsification: oscillatory structure that survives the substitution cannot have been imposed by phase-accurate knot placement. As a by-product, the difference between the two constructions gives an empirical scale for how much the estimated periods depend on the anchoring — a more defensible bound, in this setting, than a nominal standard error computed under an independence assumption that the strongly autocorrelated residuals violate.

## Separation of the non-harmonic component

Each locked trend still contains the periodic solar response. A LOESS fit of span `r LOESS_SPAN` and degree 2 (Cleveland and Devlin 1988) extracts its slowly varying, non-harmonic part. The difference between the deseasonalised anomaly and that non-harmonic part gives the harmonic residual field on which the spectral analysis is performed.

## Spectral characterisation: SSA and ESPRIT

Singular Spectrum Analysis embeds the residual series in a trajectory matrix of window length $L$ and decomposes it into eigentriples (Golyandina et al. 2001; Golyandina and Korobeynikov 2014). Components are grouped into pairs, since a damped sinusoid appears in SSA as a pair of eigenvectors in quadrature; paired scatter plots and the w-correlation matrix are used to verify separability.

For each grouped pair, ESPRIT (Roy and Kailath 1989) estimates the complex root $z = \vert z\vert e^{i 2\pi f}$, which yields simultaneously the oscillation frequency $f$ and the continuous growth or decay rate $\lambda = \ln\vert z\vert$. A modulus indistinguishable from unity indicates a stationary mode; $\vert z\vert < 1$ indicates decay over the observation window.

These estimates are **descriptive**. They characterise the oscillatory field and are used for visualisation and for the null test of Section 3.2; no reconstructed component, period or damping rate is carried into the baseline extrapolation or the growth-curve estimation that follow. That separation is deliberate: the spectral description is exploratory, and nothing downstream should inherit a grouping decision made by eye from a w-correlation matrix.

Two window lengths are used: $L = \lfloor N/2 \rfloor$ for the detrended residual field, which maximises resolution for long periods, and $L = 128$ for the decomposition of the solar-locked trend itself, which is the appropriate scale for separating its secular from its multi-decadal part.

## Baseline extrapolation and the industrial residual

The record is split at the calendar year `r SPLIT_YEAR`, on the assumption that industrial emissions had no material effect on ocean SST before that date; the training set comprises `r n_train` months. A Generalized Additive Model with a **cyclic cubic spline basis** (`bs = "cc"`, $k = `r GAM_K`$; Wood 2017) is fitted to the training set only, then evaluated over the full record. The cyclic basis is a deliberate choice and not a default: it constrains the fitted function to match in value and first derivative at the two ends of the training window, so the continuation beyond `r SPLIT_YEAR` repeats the pre-industrial pattern of variability rather than projecting its endpoint slope indefinitely. That is the appropriate constraint if the natural baseline is taken to be quasi-periodic, which is the hypothesis this study tests; it is the wrong constraint if the natural baseline carries a secular component of its own. @sec-basis-sensitivity quantifies what the alternative would do to every downstream estimate. The industrial effect is defined as

$$\mathrm{industrial}(t) \;=\; \mathrm{anomaly}(t) \;-\; \widehat{\mathrm{GAM}}_{<`r SPLIT_YEAR`}(t).$$

The split is specified as a calendar year rather than as the midpoint of the record, so that it does not move when the record length changes. It should be read as a first approximation and nothing more. There is no date at which industrial influence on ocean SST begins: the emission effect grows continuously from a level indistinguishable from zero, so any boundary drawn on the time axis is a device for separating a slow secular term from the natural harmonics, not a physical event. `r SPLIT_YEAR` is defensible on emission-history grounds, and @tbl-basis together with the split-year sensitivity listed in Appendix A bound what the choice costs; the decomposition that follows should be understood as conditional on it.

## Growth-curve models

The response of the growth-curve fit is the deseasonalised monthly anomaly with the harmonic part of the solar-locked trend removed, $y(t) = \mathrm{anomaly}(t) - [\,\mathrm{locked}(t) - \mathrm{LOESS}(\mathrm{locked})(t)\,]$. It is the non-harmonic trend of Section 3.3 with the monthly residual retained, so it carries the secular rise together with the observation noise. It is fitted first with a four-parameter symmetric logistic,

$$y(t) = b + \frac{L}{1 + e^{-k\,(t - t_0)}},$$

by Levenberg–Marquardt least squares, giving the rate coefficient $k$ and the inflection $t_0$. The symmetric logistic imposes equal curvature on the accelerating and saturating limbs, which has no physical justification for a system in which upper-ocean heat uptake, evaporation, cloud formation and albedo feedback operate on different timescales in the two phases.

The fit is therefore generalised to a Richards curve (Richards 1959),

$$y(t) = L + \frac{\Delta}{\bigl(1 + e^{-B\,(t - t_0)}\bigr)^{1/\nu}},$$

with $B$ held at the value returned by the logistic fit, so that the secular rate is not re-estimated and the two curves differ only in shape, and with $\nu$ free.

In this parametrisation $t_0$ is a **location parameter**, not the inflection point. Setting the second derivative to zero gives $e^{-B(t-t_0)} = \nu$, so the date of maximum acceleration is

$$t_{\mathrm{infl}} = t_0 - \frac{\ln \nu}{B},$$

which coincides with $t_0$ only when $\nu = 1$. All comparisons against the logistic are therefore made at the turning point rather than at $t_0$.

The observations are monthly and discrete, so the turning point is read from the fitted curve as the sample of steepest rise, `which.max(diff(.))`, rather than from the continuous root. The analytic root is reported alongside it as a consistency check; the two agree to `r sprintf("%.2f", abs(analytic_gap))` yr, well inside the monthly sampling interval.

The estimation is in two steps and nothing more: the logistic is fitted by Levenberg–Marquardt in a single call, and the Richards curve is then fitted with $B$ held at the value the logistic returned. Neither step needs bounds, a grid search, or a separate estimate of the asymptotes.

What the estimation does require is that the response retain its noise. An earlier version of this analysis fitted the growth curve to a low-pass filtered residual, `hr(y, N/1:20)`. That response is smooth over long stretches, so the sum of squares is nearly flat along the ridge that trades the upper asymptote against the rate, and the optimiser either stalls or runs to a bound — which is what motivated an elaborate staged estimator in place of the fit itself. Fitting the unfiltered monthly series removes the problem: the residual scatter breaks the degeneracy without displacing the optimum. The control is reported in Section 5.2 — refitting the smoothed non-harmonic trend alone moves $t_0$ by `r sprintf("%.2f", noise_shift_t0)` yr and $k$ by `r sprintf("%.4f", noise_shift_k)` yr$^{-1}$, so the noise changes the conditioning and not the estimate.

## Uncertainty

Three complementary bounds are reported rather than a single interval:

1.  **Parameter intervals.** For the growth-curve coefficients, standard errors are taken from the non-linear least-squares fit and propagated to $t_{\mathrm{infl}}$ by Monte Carlo sampling (20 000 draws) from the estimated parameter covariance. These are *model-conditional* and assume independent residuals; because the residuals are strongly autocorrelated, they should be read as lower bounds on the true uncertainty.
2.  **Construction spread.** The difference between the phase-locked and mean-cycle constructions (@sec-meancycle) bounds the sensitivity of the spectral estimates to the anchoring.
3.  **Structural sensitivity.** The dependence on the split year and on the extrapolation basis is discussed in Section 5.4 and is the dominant term.

## Software

All computation is performed in R. The analysis uses `Rssa` for SSA and ESPRIT, `mgcv` for the GAM, `minpack.lm` for Levenberg–Marquardt non-linear least squares, `itsmr` for seasonal adjustment and harmonic filtering, `splines` for the B-spline basis, and the `tidyverse` for data handling.

# Results

## The solar-locked trend and its non-harmonic component

The non-harmonic component of the phase-locked trend (@fig-solar-locked) has minima near `r sprintf("%.0f", Min_early)` and `r sprintf("%.0f", Min_mid)` and a turning point near `r sprintf("%.0f", Turn_late)`, marked by the vertical lines. The mean-cycle control is overlaid: the two curves differ by an RMS of `r sprintf("%.3f", rmse_constructions)` °C, so the low-frequency shape of the trend is not an artefact of phase-accurate knot placement.

```{r}
#| label: fig-solar-locked
#| fig-cap: "Non-harmonic component of the ocean solar-locked trend (LOESS, span 0.25), for knots at the observed solar minima (phase-locked) and at the mean cycle interval (control). Dashed lines mark the two minima; the dotted line marks the late turning point."
dat %>%
  dplyr::select(dt.mnth, `phase-locked` = nh_phase, `mean-cycle` = nh_meanc) %>%
  pivot_longer(-dt.mnth, names_to = "construction", values_to = "value") %>%
  ggplot(aes(dt.mnth, value, colour = construction)) +
  geom_line() +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Min_early, linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Min_mid,   linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = Turn_late, linetype = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)",
       title = "Ocean Solar-Locked Trend, non-harmonic part",
       subtitle = paste0("LOESS span = ", LOESS_SPAN,
                         "; mean cycle = ", sprintf("%.2f", mean_cycle), " yr")) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Total harmonic residual

Adding the periodic part back to the residuals recovers the total harmonic dependence of the global ocean anomaly (@fig-total-harmonic).

```{r}
#| label: fig-total-harmonic
#| fig-cap: "Deseasonalised anomaly band-passed to periods between 3 and 88 years (blue) against the non-harmonic trend (red), phase-locked construction."
dat %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = hr(res_phase, N / 2:60), colour = "band-pass 3–88 yr")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = nh_phase, colour = "non-harmonic trend")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Anomaly and non-harmonic trend") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Low-pass structure of the residuals

Low-pass filtering the residuals at cut-off periods of 5, 11 and 15 years (@fig-lowpass) shows that all three retained bands are dominated by the eleven-year sunspot cycle. The response of SST to solar irradiance depends on the area and depth of each ocean basin through its effective heat capacity, so the global average is a superposition of frequency-dependent regional responses. Two features survive that averaging: a deep trough with its minimum near 1911, and a second depression between approximately 1940 and 1960.

```{r}
#| label: fig-lowpass
#| fig-cap: "Anomaly residuals retained above cut-off periods of 5, 11 and 15 years (phase-locked construction)."
dat <- dat %>%
  mutate(long5  = hr(res_phase, N / 1:35),
         long11 = hr(res_phase, N / 1:16),
         long15 = hr(res_phase, N / 1:12))

dat %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = long5,  colour = "> 5 yr"), linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = long11, colour = "> 11 yr")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = long15, colour = "> 15 yr")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)", colour = "cut-off",
       title = "Anomaly residuals: long periods") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

## Eigentriple structure of the detrended field

Paired scatter plots of the leading SSA eigenvectors (@fig-ssa-paired) show the circular patterns that identify clean harmonic pairs.

```{r}
#| label: ssa-both
#| include: false
L_res <- floor(N / 2)

s_phase <- ssa(dat$res_phase, L = L_res)
s_meanc <- ssa(dat$res_meanc, L = L_res)

seltd_grps <- list(
  Pair_1_2  = c(1, 2),
  Pair_3_4  = c(3, 4),
  Pair_5_6  = c(5, 6),
  Pair_7_8  = c(7, 8),
  Pair_9_10 = c(9, 10)
)

esprit_tbl <- function(s) {
  res <- as_par_list(parestimate(s, groups = seltd_grps, method = "esprit"))
  map_dfr(res, ~ tibble(
    frequency = unlist(.x$frequencies)[1],
    rate      = unlist(.x$rates)[1],
    modulus   = unlist(.x$moduli)[1]
  ), .id = "Group") %>%
    mutate(period_months = 1 / frequency,
           period_years  = period_months / 12)
}

esp_phase <- esprit_tbl(s_phase)
esp_meanc <- esprit_tbl(s_meanc)

esp_cmp <- esp_phase %>%
  dplyr::select(Group, T_phase = period_years, mod_phase = modulus, rate_phase = rate) %>%
  left_join(esp_meanc %>% dplyr::select(Group, T_mean = period_years, mod_mean = modulus),
            by = "Group") %>%
  mutate(dT = T_phase - T_mean)

getT <- function(g) esp_phase$period_years[esp_phase$Group == g]
T12 <- getT("Pair_1_2"); T34 <- getT("Pair_3_4"); T56 <- getT("Pair_5_6")
T78 <- getT("Pair_7_8"); T910 <- getT("Pair_9_10")
mod12 <- esp_phase$modulus[esp_phase$Group == "Pair_1_2"]
max_dT <- max(abs(esp_cmp$dT), na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-ssa-paired
#| fig-cap: "Paired eigenvector scatter plots of the detrended residual field, phase-locked construction. Circular trajectories indicate well-separated harmonic pairs."
plot(s_phase, type = "paired")
```

## ESPRIT parameter estimates and the mean-cycle control

@tbl-esprit gives the period, damping rate and modulus of the five leading grouped pairs for the phase-locked construction, alongside the period recovered by the mean-cycle control.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-esprit
#| tbl-cap: "ESPRIT estimates for the five leading eigentriple pairs. T(phase) uses knots at the observed solar minima; T(mean) uses knots at the mean cycle interval. The last column is the difference between the two constructions and serves as an empirical uncertainty scale."
esp_cmp %>%
  transmute(
    `Eigentriple pair` = str_replace_all(str_remove(Group, "Pair_"), "_", ","),
    `T phase-locked (yr)` = round(T_phase, 2),
    `T mean-cycle (yr)`   = round(T_mean, 2),
    `Delta T (yr)`        = round(dT, 2),
    `Modulus |z|`         = round(mod_phase, 5),
    `Rate lambda`         = round(rate_phase, 5)
  ) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

Three regimes emerge, and the group indices below are those of @tbl-esprit rather than a separate numbering.

**Bidecadal / Hale magnetic mode — pair (1,2).** The leading pair isolates a low-frequency cycle at $T = `r sprintf("%.1f", T12)`$ yr with modulus $\vert z\vert = `r sprintf("%.5f", mod12)`$, stationary to within estimation error, consistent with solar-magnetic forcing on the \~22-year Hale cycle acting jointly with intrinsic bidecadal ocean variability. With only about `r sprintf("%.0f", (rec_to - rec_from)/T12)` realisations in the record, the damping rate of this mode is weakly constrained and the near-unit modulus should not be read as a demonstration of exact stationarity.

**Split Schwabe solar band — pairs (3,4) and (5,6).** The eleven-year band resolves into twin sidebands at $T = `r sprintf("%.1f", T34)`$ yr and $T = `r sprintf("%.1f", T56)`$ yr. A doublet of this kind is the spectral signature of amplitude and phase modulation of a single carrier across the observation window rather than of two independent oscillators.

**Interannual recharge-oscillator band — pairs (7,8) and (9,10).** The higher-frequency pairs resolve $T = `r sprintf("%.1f", T78)`$ yr and $T = `r sprintf("%.1f", T910)`$ yr, within the characteristic bandwidth of the equatorial Pacific recharge oscillator (Jin 1997) and of interannual climate modes more generally. These are the pairs actually grouped in the code as `Pair_7_8` and `Pair_9_10`; earlier drafts of this analysis mislabelled them as pairs (4,5).

The mean-cycle control recovers the same band structure, with a maximum period difference of `r sprintf("%.2f", max_dT)` yr across the five pairs (@tbl-esprit, column *Delta T*). The oscillatory content is therefore a property of the SST record and not an artefact of anchoring the spline to the observed solar minima; the phase-accurate anchoring sharpens the estimate but does not create the modes.

## SSA decomposition of the solar-locked trend

Decomposing the phase-locked trend itself ($L = 128$) separates a secular component from multi-decadal and decadal oscillations (@fig-ssa-trend).

```{r}
#| label: fig-ssa-trend
#| fig-cap: "SSA of the solar-locked trend (L = 128)."
#| fig-subcap:
#|   - "Singular-value spectrum (log scale)."
#|   - "W-correlation matrix of the first ten eigenvectors."
#|   - "Reconstruction into secular, multi-decadal and decadal parts."
#| layout-ncol: 2
L <- 128
s_sol <- ssa(dat$trd_phase, L = L)

df_values <- tibble(
  Component = seq_along(s_sol$sigma),
  SingularValue = s_sol$sigma
)

print(
  ggplot(df_values[1:20, ], aes(Component, SingularValue)) +
    geom_point(color = "steelblue", size = 2) +
    geom_line(color = "steelblue") +
    scale_y_log10() +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:20) +
    labs(title = "SSA singular values (log scale)", x = "Component index", y = "Sigma") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
)

w_mat <- as.matrix(wcor(s_sol, groups = 1:10))
print(
  expand.grid(F1 = 1:10, F2 = 1:10) %>%
    mutate(value = abs(as.vector(w_mat))) %>%
    ggplot(aes(F1, F2, fill = value)) +
    geom_tile() +
    scale_fill_gradient(low = "white", high = "blue", limits = c(0, 1)) +
    scale_x_continuous(breaks = 1:10, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    scale_y_continuous(breaks = 1:10, expand = c(0, 0)) +
    coord_fixed() +
    labs(title = "W-correlation matrix", x = "Eigenvector index", y = "Eigenvector index",
         fill = "w-cor") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11) +
    theme(panel.grid = element_blank())
)

rec <- reconstruct(s_sol, groups = list(
  Secular_Trend = c(1),
  Multidecadal  = c(2, 3),
  Decadal       = c(4, 5)
))

print(
  tibble(dt.mnth = dat$dt.mnth,
         locked = dat$trd_phase,
         Secular = rec$Secular_Trend,
         Oscillatory = rec$Multidecadal + rec$Decadal) %>%
    ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
    geom_line(aes(y = locked, colour = "solar-locked trend")) +
    geom_line(aes(y = Secular, colour = "secular"), linewidth = 1.2) +
    geom_line(aes(y = Oscillatory, colour = "multidecadal + decadal")) +
    labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)", colour = NULL, title = "SSA-decomposed solar trend") +
    theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
)
```

## Baseline extrapolation and the industrial residual

The alternative decomposition retained here for comparison is constructed in four steps:

1.  the record is split at `r SPLIT_YEAR`, and the earlier part (`r n_train` months) is used as the GAM training set;
2.  the fitted GAM is evaluated over the full record length, and this extension is taken to represent the natural anomaly in the absence of industrial influence;
3.  the difference between observation and extension defines the industrial effect, which is by construction near zero well before `r SPLIT_YEAR`;
4.  that residual is fitted with the same two-step estimator as the solar-locked response — a symmetric logistic to establish the secular rate, then a Richards curve at fixed rate, on the physical argument that the approach to saturation is governed by different processes from the initial phase — evaporation at elevated temperature, cloud formation and albedo response among them.

Both decompositions are carried through to @tbl-aic, where they are scored against the same response.

```{r}
#| label: fig-preind-split
#| fig-cap: "Extrapolated pre-1938 baseline (GAM, cyclic cubic spline, k = 30) and the low-pass filtered industrial residual. The cyclic basis is periodic on the span of its training window, so the extension after 1938 repeats the pre-industrial pattern at an interval of exactly that span; the spacing of its two minima is therefore fixed by the choice of split year and carries no information about any physical cycle."
df_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = extrapol_pre, colour = "GAM baseline (trained < 1938)")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = industr.smth, colour = "industrial residual, smoothed")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = SPLIT_YEAR, linetype = 3) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Anomaly split at the training boundary") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-logistic
#| fig-cap: "Four-parameter logistic fit to the deseasonalised anomaly with the harmonic part of the solar-locked trend removed, with lower and upper asymptotes and the turning point."
df_results %>%
  mutate(growth = df_full$growth) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = growth, colour = "observed - harmonic"), alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(aes(y = logist_fit, colour = "logistic"), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = lower_asymptote, linetype = 2, colour = "blue") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = upper_asymptote, linetype = 2, colour = "red") +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_turn_log, linetype = 3) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Anomaly effect (°C)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Industrial growth curve, solar-locked construction",
       subtitle = paste0("turning point (steepest rise): ", sprintf("%.1f", t_turn_log),
                         "; span reached by ", sprintf("%.0f", rec_to), ": ",
                         sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * span_reached))) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-compare-fits
#| fig-cap: "Symmetric logistic against the Richards curve fitted at fixed rate coefficient. The dotted line marks the Richards inflection, the dashed line the logistic inflection."
df_results %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = logist_fit, colour = "logistic")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = richardsB,  colour = "Richards (fixed B)")) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_turn_log,  linetype = 2) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = t_turn_rich, linetype = 3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = lower_asymptote.rich, linetype = 2, colour = "red") +
  geom_hline(yintercept = upper_asymptote.rich, linetype = 2, colour = "darkgreen") +
```
