## Turning point and the effect of releasing symmetry

@tbl-turning reports the location parameters of the two fits together with the inflection date of the Richards curve. Only the inflection dates are directly comparable.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-turning
#| tbl-cap: "Location parameters, shape and turning points of the symmetric and asymmetric fits to the solar-locked response. The slope is estimated once, in step 1, and held fixed in step 2, so the two curves differ only in shape. Intervals are model-conditional and assume independent residuals."
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Lower asymptote b (°C)",
               "Upper asymptote U (°C)",
               "Slope B, step 1 (yr^-1)",
               "Turning point, symmetric (yr)",
               "Shape nu, step 2",
               "Turning point, asymmetric (yr)",
               "Shift, asymmetric - symmetric (yr)",
               "Analytic root t0 - ln(nu)/B (yr)",
               "Steepest rise of the observed non-harmonic trend (yr)"),
  Value = c(say(lower_asymptote, "%.3f"),
            say(upper_asymptote, "%.3f"),
            say(B_fixed, "%.4f"),
            say(t_turn_log, "%.1f"),
            say(nu_hat, "%.3f"),
            say(t_turn_rich, "%.1f"),
            say(infl_shift, "%+.1f"),
            say(t_infl_rich, "%.1f"),
            sprintf("%.1f", t_turn_obs)),
  `95% interval` = c("—", "—", "—",
                     if (growth_ok) fmt_ci(ci_t0log) else "—",
                     "—", "—", "—", "—", "—"),
  Interpretation = c("Logistic constant term",
                     "b + L; an extrapolation, see 'span reached' below",
                     "Estimated in step 1, held fixed in step 2",
                     "Sample of steepest rise of the symmetric fit",
                     "nu < 1 means an earlier, sharper acceleration limb",
                     "Sample of steepest rise of the asymmetric fit",
                     "Negative means the asymmetric curve turns earlier",
                     "Continuous-time check on the discrete reading",
                     "Model-free: steepest rise of the LOESS non-harmonic trend")
) %>% kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "l"))
```

The record covers only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * span_reached)` of the fitted span, so the upper asymptote in @tbl-turning is a property of the extrapolated curve and not a quantity the data constrain. The turning point, which lies inside or close to the observation window, is the estimate this analysis can defend; the ceiling is not.

## Which decomposition the data prefer {#sec-aic}

The two decompositions — the solar-locked construction of Section 3.1 and the extrapolated GAM baseline of Section 3.6 — imply different responses, so their growth-curve fits cannot be compared by a residual sum of squares over those responses. They can be compared as models of the same quantity, the deseasonalised anomaly, by scoring the full reconstruction

$$\widehat{\mathrm{anomaly}}(t) = \underbrace{\text{smooth/periodic part}}_{\text{harmonic part, or GAM baseline}} \; + \; \underbrace{\text{growth curve}}_{\text{logistic or Richards}}$$

against that anomaly, counting the effective degrees of freedom of the smoothing step. @tbl-aic reports both readings: `AIC (series)` compares the logistic and the Richards fit within each route and is exact; `AIC (anomaly)` compares the four reconstructions against the same response and is approximate, because the LOESS and GAM degrees of freedom are effective rather than exact. Differences of a few units in the second column should not be over-read.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-aic
#| tbl-cap: "Growth-curve fits under the two decompositions. AIC (series) is computed on each route's own response and compares only the two growth curves within a route. AIC (anomaly) scores the full reconstruction against the deseasonalised anomaly and is comparable across all four rows, with the effective degrees of freedom of the smoothing step included. 'Span' is the fraction of the fitted sigmoid the record actually covers."
aic_tbl %>%
  transmute(Route, `Growth curve` = Growth,
            `AIC (series)`  = round(AIC_series, 1),
            `AIC (anomaly)` = round(AIC_anomaly, 1),
            `dAIC`          = round(dAIC_anomaly, 1),
            `k (yr^-1)`     = round(k, 4),
            `Turning point` = round(turn, 1),
            `nu`            = ifelse(is.na(nu), "\u2014", sprintf("%.3f", nu)),
            `Ceiling (°C)`  = round(ceiling, 3),
            `Span`          = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reached)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

On this criterion the preferred reconstruction is the **`r aic_best_route`** route with the **`r aic_best_growth`** growth curve. Within the solar-locked route, releasing the symmetry constraint changes AIC by `r sprintf("%+.1f", dAIC_richards_A)`; a difference of that size is weak evidence for asymmetry rather than a decision between the two shapes, and the honest statement is that the record does not strongly distinguish them. The criterion answers only the question it is designed to answer — which model predicts the observed anomaly best per parameter spent — and it cannot adjudicate the physical question of whether the natural baseline is quasi-periodic, because that assumption enters both routes before any fitting takes place.

## Mean versus median construction {#sec-median}

The global series can be formed as an area- and ocean-fraction-weighted mean of the grid cells or as the corresponding weighted median. The whole construction — locked trend, LOESS, growth curve — is repeated on the median series in @tbl-median.

```{r}
#| label: median-control
#| include: false

med <- Ocean_NOAA.data$data %>%
  dplyr::select(dt.mnth, Anomaly = anoma.median) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dt.mnth >= RECORD_START) %>%
  inner_join(dplyr::select(solar_mnthly, dt.mnth, SI), by = "dt.mnth") %>%
  arrange(dt.mnth) %>%
  mutate(anomaly = Resid(Anomaly, M.ssn))

trd_med <- as.numeric(predict(
  lm(Anomaly ~ bs(dt.mnth, knots = nodes_obs_in, degree = 3), data = med)))
nh_med  <- as.numeric(predict(loess(trd_med ~ med$dt.mnth,
                                    span = LOESS_SPAN, degree = 2)))
growth_med <- med$anomaly - (trd_med - nh_med)
fitM <- fit_growth(growth_med, med$dt.mnth)

cmp_tbl <- tibble(
  Quantity = c("Slope k (yr^-1)", "Logistic t0 (yr)", "Logistic turning point (yr)",
               "Richards shape nu", "Richards turning point (yr)",
               "Span L (K)", "Ceiling (K)", "Span of the sigmoid reached (%)",
               "sd of the natural component (K)"),
  Mean   = c(fitA$k, fitA$t0_log, fitA$turn_log, fitA$nu, fitA$turn_rich,
             fitA$L, fitA$upper_r, 100 * fitA$reached,
             sd(dat$anomaly - df_results$richardsB)),
  Median = c(fitM$k, fitM$t0_log, fitM$turn_log, fitM$nu, fitM$turn_rich,
             fitM$L, fitM$upper_r, 100 * fitM$reached,
             sd(med$anomaly - fitM$y_rich)))

cor_trend   <- cor(nh_phase_vec <- dat$nh_phase, nh_med)
cor_natural <- cor(dat$anomaly - df_results$richardsB, med$anomaly - fitM$y_rich)
ceiling_ratio <- fitM$upper_r / fitA$upper_r
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-median
#| tbl-cap: "The same construction applied to the weighted mean and to the weighted median of the grid cells. Timing and shape agree; amplitude does not."
cmp_tbl %>%
  mutate(across(c(Mean, Median), ~ signif(.x, 4)),
         Difference = signif(Median - Mean, 3)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The timing is robust and the amplitude is not. The rate coefficient, the inflection and the shape parameter agree between the two constructions to well inside the interval quoted in @tbl-turning, and the non-harmonic trends correlate at `r sprintf("%.4f", cor_trend)`. The fitted span, however, is larger by a factor of `r sprintf("%.2f", ceiling_ratio)` in the median series, and the natural components correlate only at `r sprintf("%.2f", cor_natural)`.

That difference is a property of the statistic and not of the ocean. The spatial distribution of sea surface temperature is broad and strongly structured — warm tropics, cold high latitudes — so its median lies on a steep part of the distribution and responds to changes in the shape of that distribution and in cell coverage, not only to a shift of its centre. A spatial median is therefore not a robust version of a spatial mean here; it is a different quantity, and a more coverage-sensitive one. The area-weighted mean is used throughout for that reason, and the median is reported as the sensitivity it is. What the comparison establishes is that the dates in @tbl-turning do not depend on the choice, while any statement about the magnitude of the ceiling does.

## Dependence on the analysis window {#sec-window}

The construction of Section 3.1 contains no window length, bandwidth or split year, so its output should not move when the analysis window does. That is a testable claim and @tbl-window tests it, by repeating the whole construction on sub-windows of the record and comparing the results over the span the windows share.

```{r}
#| label: window-sensitivity
#| include: false

refit_window <- function(from, to) {
  w  <- oc %>% dplyr::filter(dt.mnth >= from, dt.mnth <= to)
  nd <- w$dt.mnth[find_nodes(w$Solar_Variation)]
  nd <- nd[nd > min(w$dt.mnth) & nd < max(w$dt.mnth)]
  trd <- as.numeric(predict(lm(Anomaly ~ bs(dt.mnth, knots = nd, degree = 3), data = w)))
  nh  <- as.numeric(predict(loess(trd ~ w$dt.mnth, span = LOESS_SPAN, degree = 2)))
  g   <- w$anomaly - (trd - nh)
  f   <- fit_growth(g, w$dt.mnth)
  list(t = w$dt.mnth, trd = trd, nh = nh, fit = f, knots = length(nd))
}

windows <- list(c(RECORD_START, rec_to), c(1870, rec_to), c(1890, rec_to), c(1910, rec_to),
                c(RECORD_START, 2015), c(RECORD_START, 1995), c(RECORD_START, 1985))
W <- map(windows, ~ refit_window(.x[1], .x[2]))
Wfull <- W[[1]]

## growth-curve parameters under each window
win_tbl <- map2_dfr(W, windows, function(w, lim) {
  f <- w$fit
  tibble(window = sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", lim[1], lim[2]),
         knots = w$knots,
         k = if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else f$k,
         turn_log  = if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else f$turn_log,
         nu        = if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else f$nu,
         turn_rich = if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else f$turn_rich,
         ceiling   = if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else f$upper_r,
         span      = if (is.null(f)) NA_real_ else 100 * f$reached)
})

## stability of the trend itself, compared on the shared span with ten years
## trimmed at each end to keep the comparison away from the spline boundaries
trend_cmp <- map2_dfr(W[-1], windows[-1], function(w, lim) {
  lo <- max(min(Wfull$t), min(w$t)) + 10
  hi <- min(max(Wfull$t), max(w$t)) - 10
  i1 <- Wfull$t >= lo & Wfull$t <= hi
  i2 <- w$t     >= lo & w$t     <= hi
  n  <- min(sum(i1), sum(i2))
  tibble(window = sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", lim[1], lim[2]),
         overlap = sprintf("%.0f-%.0f", lo, hi),
         rms_nh  = sd(Wfull$nh[i1][seq_len(n)]  - w$nh[i2][seq_len(n)]),
         cor_nh  = cor(Wfull$nh[i1][seq_len(n)],  w$nh[i2][seq_len(n)]),
         rms_trd = sd(Wfull$trd[i1][seq_len(n)] - w$trd[i2][seq_len(n)]))
})
rms_worst <- max(trend_cmp$rms_nh)
cor_worst <- min(trend_cmp$cor_nh)
turn_range <- range(win_tbl$turn_rich, na.rm = TRUE)
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-window
#| tbl-cap: "Left: the non-harmonic solar-locked trend recomputed on sub-windows and compared with the full-record trend over the span they share, ten years trimmed at each end. Right: the growth-curve parameters obtained from each of those windows."
trend_cmp %>%
  transmute(Window = window, `Compared over` = overlap,
            `RMS difference, non-harmonic (K)` = round(rms_nh, 4),
            `Correlation` = round(cor_nh, 4),
            `RMS difference, locked trend (K)` = round(rms_trd, 4)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "l", "r", "r", "r"))

win_tbl %>%
  transmute(Window = window, Knots = knots,
            `k (yr^-1)` = round(k, 4),
            `Turning point, logistic` = round(turn_log, 1),
            `nu` = round(nu, 3),
            `Turning point, Richards` = round(turn_rich, 1),
            `Ceiling (K)` = round(ceiling, 2),
            `Span reached` = sprintf("%.0f%%", span)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r", "r"))
```

The two halves of @tbl-window answer differently, and the difference is the point.

**The trend construction is window-independent, as intended.** Recomputed on windows starting up to sixty years later or ending up to forty years earlier, the non-harmonic solar-locked trend differs from the full-record version by at most `r sprintf("%.3f", rms_worst)` K RMS over the shared span, with correlations no lower than `r sprintf("%.4f", cor_worst)`. Nothing in the construction has to be chosen, so there is nothing for the answer to depend on: the knots are where the Sun puts them, and adding or removing years at either end adds or removes knots without moving the ones that remain. This is the property the construction was adopted for, and it holds.

**The growth curve fitted to that trend is not window-independent.** Across the same windows the Richards turning point ranges over `r sprintf("%.0f", turn_range[1])`–`r sprintf("%.0f", turn_range[2])` and the ceiling by more than a factor of two; truncating the record at 1890 leaves the sigmoid unidentified altogether. That instability has a single cause and it is not the trend construction: the record reaches only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * span_reached)` of the fitted sigmoid, and every truncation makes that worse. A saturating curve fitted to a series that has not saturated has little information about where it saturates, so its asymptote and inflection move with the last point observed. The same would happen to any growth curve fitted to any trend, however that trend was obtained.

The practical consequence is a division of what this study can and cannot claim. The decomposition into a non-harmonic trend and an oscillatory field is robust to the analysis window and does not use a split year at all — `SPLIT_YEAR` enters only the alternative baseline of Section 3.6, which is carried for comparison in @tbl-aic and is not the source of any headline number. The parameters of the growth curve fitted afterwards are conditional on the record ending when it does, and should be read as a description of the observed rise rather than as an estimate of where it is going.

## The decomposition and its low-pass view

@fig-decomposition shows the observed anomaly with its pre-industrial and industrial parts; @fig-decomposition-lowpass repeats the comparison after low-pass filtering at a cut-off period near nine years, with the fitted industrial model superimposed.

```{r}
#| label: baseline-sensitivity
#| include: false

## The same two-step estimator applied to the residual produced by each
## candidate baseline, so the comparison is of baselines and not of fitting
## procedures.
baseline_variant <- function(kk, bs_name) {
  g  <- tryCatch(mgcv::gam(anomaly ~ s(dt.mnth, k = kk, bs = bs_name), data = df_train),
                 error = function(e) NULL)
  if (is.null(g)) return(NULL)
  pr <- as.numeric(predict(g, newdata = df_full))
  ie <- df_full$anomaly - pr
  r  <- fit_growth(ie, tt)
  if (is.null(r)) {
    return(tibble(basis = bs_name, k = kk, rate = NA_real_, t0 = NA_real_,
                  upper = NA_real_, reached = NA_real_, identified = FALSE,
                  ie_2026 = tail(ie, 1)))
  }
  tibble(basis = bs_name, k = kk, rate = r$k, t0 = r$turn_log,
         upper = r$upper, reached = r$reached,
         identified = is.finite(r$k) && r$k > 0.005 && r$reached > 0.9,
         ie_2026 = tail(ie, 1))
}

sens_grid <- list(c(30, "cc"), c(12, "cc"), c(30, "cr"), c(6, "cr"))
sens_tbl <- map_dfr(sens_grid, ~ baseline_variant(as.numeric(.x[1]), .x[2]))
```

## Sensitivity of the industrial fit to the baseline basis {#sec-basis-sensitivity}

The industrial component is defined entirely by the extrapolated baseline, so the choice of spline basis is not a technical detail. @tbl-basis reports the logistic fit obtained under four baselines: the cyclic basis used here at two flexibilities and the non-cyclic cubic regression spline at two. Every variant is fitted by the free search from data-driven starting values, so the table reports each baseline's least-squares optimum rather than the constrained solution of @tbl-turning.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-basis
#| tbl-cap: "Logistic fit to the industrial residual under four GAM baselines, all fitted with the same two-step estimator. The last-but-one column gives the fraction of the fitted span the record actually covers; well below 100 per cent means the upper asymptote is an extrapolation rather than an estimate."
sens_tbl %>%
  transmute(Basis = basis, k = k,
            `Slope B` = round(rate, 4),
            `Turning point (yr)` = round(t0, 1),
            `Span reached by 2026` = ifelse(is.na(reached), "\u2014", sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * reached)),
            `Residual at 2026 (°C)` = round(ie_2026, 3)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r", "r", "l", "r"))
```

The two cyclic variants agree with one another to within `r sprintf("%.1f", diff(range(sens_tbl$t0[sens_tbl$basis == "cc"], na.rm = TRUE)))` yr despite a factor of `r round(max(sens_tbl$k[sens_tbl$basis == "cc"]) / min(sens_tbl$k[sens_tbl$basis == "cc"]), 1)` in basis dimension, so within that family the estimate is not sensitive to how flexible the baseline is. The non-cyclic variants behave differently, and the diagnostic column to watch is the span: where it stays well below 100 per cent the curve is still climbing at the end of the record and the asymptote is carried entirely by the functional form. The last column is diagnostic of the extrapolation itself — a residual far from zero at the end of the record means the baseline has drifted away from the observations, and the value of `r sprintf("%.2f", sens_tbl$ie_2026[sens_tbl$basis == "cr" & sens_tbl$k == 30])` °C for the 30-knot non-cyclic baseline shows how badly a flexible spline can behave when extrapolated. The mechanism is discussed in @sec-growth-identifiability.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decomposition
#| fig-cap: "Observed anomaly decomposed into the extrapolated pre-industrial baseline and the industrial residual."
df_final %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = anomaly, colour = "observed anomaly")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pre_ind, colour = "pre-industrial baseline")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = industrial_effect, colour = "industrial residual")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Industrial and natural components") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

Three features are visible before filtering:

- as the extrapolated natural baseline falls from about 1950 to about 2000, the natural component subtracts from the observed rise;
- after 2000 the natural component rises again and contributes to a steeper observed increase;
- the industrial component itself turns to a slower ascent over the same period.

```{r}
#| label: fig-decomposition-lowpass
#| fig-cap: "Low-pass filtered decomposition (cut-off period near nine years) with the fitted industrial model superimposed."
df_final %>%
  mutate(anoma.long = hr(anomaly, N / 1:20),
         indus.long = hr(industrial_effect, N / 1:20)) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dt.mnth > rec_from + 1, dt.mnth < 2025) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = anoma.long, colour = "observed (low-pass)")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = pre_ind,    colour = "pre-industrial baseline")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = indus.long, colour = "industrial (low-pass)")) +
  geom_line(aes(y = indus.trend, colour = "fitted industrial model"), linewidth = 1.2) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (°C)", colour = NULL,
       title = "Decomposition, low-pass filtered") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 11)
```

```{r}
#| label: trough-stats
#| include: false
pre_lp <- df_final %>% mutate(pre_lp = pre_ind)
trough_early <- pre_lp %>% dplyr::filter(dt.mnth < 1930) %>% slice_min(pre_lp, n = 1)
trough_late  <- pre_lp %>% dplyr::filter(dt.mnth > 1980) %>% slice_min(pre_lp, n = 1)

## The extrapolated baseline uses a CYCLIC basis, which is periodic on the span
## of its training window by construction.  Any repeat interval the extension
## shows is therefore set by where the record was split, not by the ocean.
## Measure it rather than assume it.
train_span  <- SPLIT_YEAR - RECORD_START
trough_gap  <- trough_late$dt.mnth - trough_early$dt.mnth
gap_vs_span <- trough_gap - train_span
```

# Discussion

## Phase interaction between natural variability and forcing

The decomposition exposes a phase relationship rather than a simple superposition of magnitudes. The extrapolated pre-industrial baseline reaches a first minimum of `r sprintf("%.2f", trough_early$pre_lp)` °C near `r sprintf("%.0f", trough_early$dt.mnth)` and a second of `r sprintf("%.2f", trough_late$pre_lp)` °C near `r sprintf("%.0f", trough_late$dt.mnth)`. The second coincides with the interval over which the industrial component is accelerating most rapidly.

Those two minima are separated by `r sprintf("%.0f", trough_gap)` yr. That is close to the Gleissberg cycle conventionally quoted at 88 yr, and it is tempting to read it as one — but it is also within `r sprintf("%.1f", abs(gap_vs_span))` yr of the `r sprintf("%.0f", train_span)`-yr span of the GAM training window. The cyclic basis is periodic on that span by construction, so the spacing of the minima in @fig-preind-split is set by where the record was split and not by anything in the ocean. It is worth stating explicitly, because the coincidence is easy to over-read; it is also the reason the feature does not reappear in @fig-natural, where the solar-locked route uses no extrapolated baseline and nothing carries the training-window period. @tbl-windows returns to this.

The consequence is destructive interference. Through the second half of the twentieth century the observed anomaly rises more slowly than the industrial component alone would imply, because the natural component is falling over the same interval; after 2000 the sign reverses and the natural component reinforces the observed rise. On this reading the moderated slope of the late twentieth century is a phase artefact of the natural cycles rather than a deceleration of forcing — an interpretation consistent in direction with analyses attributing the 1998–2013 moderation to Pacific decadal variability (Kosaka and Xie 2013; Medhaug et al. 2017), though reached here without prescribing an index of that variability.

## The natural component outside the observation window {#sec-natural-extrap}

```{r}
#| label: natural-extrap
#| include: false

natural    <- dat$anomaly - df_results$richardsB
sd_natural <- sd(natural)
REC_LEN    <- rec_to - rec_from

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## How much of the component can be carried at all.  Everything below about
## two years is weather and interannual noise; no deterministic model should
## be expected to reproduce it, so the coverage of a model is quoted both
## against the total and against the part above that cut-off.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
lowpass <- function(x, cut_yr) {
  n <- length(x); X <- fft(x)
  fr <- c(0:(n %/% 2), -((n - n %/% 2 - 1):1)) / n * 12
  X[abs(fr) > 1 / cut_yr] <- 0
  Re(fft(X, inverse = TRUE)) / n
}
nat_lp   <- lowpass(natural, 2)
frac_low <- var(nat_lp) / var(natural)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Primary model: SSA reconstruction, extrapolated by its linear recurrence.
## A subspace reconstruction represents a modulated carrier, which a
## fixed-frequency regression cannot; the window is chosen long enough for the
## multidecadal band and short enough for a stable LRR.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
L_nat  <- 480
R_COMP <- 30
s_nat  <- ssa(natural, L = L_nat)
rec_nat <- as.numeric(reconstruct(s_nat, groups = list(H = 1:R_COMP))$H)
cov_total <- var(rec_nat) / var(natural)
cov_low   <- 1 - var(nat_lp - rec_nat) / var(nat_lp)
noise_sd  <- sd(natural - rec_nat)

h_fwd <- round((2100 - rec_to) * 12)
h_bwd <- round((rec_from - 1600) * 12)
ssa_fwd <- as.numeric(unlist(rforecast(s_nat, groups = list(1:R_COMP),
                                       len = h_fwd, only.new = TRUE)))
s_rev   <- ssa(rev(natural), L = L_nat)
ssa_bwd <- rev(as.numeric(unlist(rforecast(s_rev, groups = list(1:R_COMP),
                                           len = h_bwd, only.new = TRUE))))
t_fwd <- rec_to + seq_len(h_fwd) / 12
t_bwd <- rec_from - rev(seq_len(h_bwd)) / 12
## a recurrent forecast diverges if the LRR has roots outside the unit circle;
## check rather than assume
lrr_stable <- max(abs(ssa_fwd)) < 5 * sd_natural && max(abs(ssa_bwd)) < 5 * sd_natural

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Comparison model: fixed-period synthesis with zero damping.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
pairs_nat <- split(1:24, rep(1:12, each = 2)); names(pairs_nat) <- paste0("P", 1:12)
s_nat_full <- ssa(natural, L = floor(N / 2))       # long window: period estimates
pe_nat <- as_par_list(parestimate(s_nat_full, groups = pairs_nat, method = "esprit"))
mode_tbl <- imap_dfr(pe_nat, ~ tibble(
  group   = .y,
  period  = esprit_period(.x),
  modulus = unlist(.x$moduli)[1])) %>%
  mutate(share = map_dbl(pairs_nat,
                         ~ sum(s_nat_full$sigma[.x]^2) / sum(s_nat_full$sigma^2)))
per_fix <- mode_tbl %>% dplyr::filter(period >= 2.5, period <= REC_LEN) %>%
  pull(period) %>% round(2) %>% unique() %>% sort()

harm_design <- function(x, P) do.call(cbind, lapply(P, function(p)
  cbind(cos(2 * pi * x / p), sin(2 * pi * x / p))))
m_fix    <- lm(natural ~ harm_design(time, per_fix))
fix_in   <- as.numeric(predict(m_fix))
pred_fix <- function(x) as.numeric(cbind(1, harm_design(x, per_fix)) %*% coef(m_fix))
cov_fix_total <- var(fix_in) / var(natural)
cov_fix_low   <- 1 - var(nat_lp - fix_in) / var(nat_lp)

## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
## Is the longest mode a property of the ocean or of the detrending?  The
## component is a residual, so a mismatch between the fitted growth curve and
## the true secular part lands in the longest available mode.  Remove the
## secular part in structurally different ways and see what survives.
## --------------------------------------------------------------------------
lead_period <- function(r) {
  sr <- ssa(r, L = floor(N / 2))   # long window, period estimation only
  pp <- as_par_list(parestimate(sr, groups = list(1:2), method = "esprit"))
  tibble(period = esprit_period(pp[[1]]),
         share  = sum(sr$sigma[1:2]^2) / sum(sr$sigma^2))
}
detrend_tbl <- bind_rows(
  lead_period(dat$anomaly - df_results$richardsB)         %>% mutate(removal = "Richards curve"),
  lead_period(dat$anomaly - df_results$logist_fit)        %>% mutate(removal = "logistic curve"),
  lead_period(dat$anomaly - dat$nh_phase)                 %>% mutate(removal = "LOESS non-harmonic trend"),
  lead_period(residuals(lm(dat$anomaly ~ poly(time, 3)))) %>% mutate(removal = "cubic polynomial"),
  lead_period(residuals(lm(dat$anomaly ~ time)))          %>% mutate(removal = "straight line")
) %>% dplyr::select(removal, period, share)
per_range <- range(detrend_tbl$period)

## and: does the solar proxy itself carry a mode of comparable length?  Its
## record is longer than the SST one, so it constrains long periods better.
s_sol_full <- ssa(solar_mnthly$SI, L = floor(nrow(solar_mnthly) / 2))
pe_sol <- as_par_list(parestimate(s_sol_full, groups = split(1:12, rep(1:6, each = 2)),
                                  method = "esprit"))
sol_long <- map_dbl(pe_sol, esprit_period) %>% max()
sol_span <- diff(range(solar_mnthly$dt.mnth))

## results
LIA    <- c(1645, 1725)
in_lia <- t_bwd >= LIA[1] & t_bwd <= LIA[2]
lia_mean <- mean(ssa_bwd[in_lia]); lia_min <- min(ssa_bwd[in_lia]); lia_max <- max(ssa_bwd[in_lia])
fix_lia  <- pred_fix(t_bwd[in_lia])
richards_ext <- function(x) {
  cr <- coef(fitA$rich)
  cr[["Lr"]] + cr[["Delta"]] / (1 + exp(-fitA$k * (x - cr[["t0r"]])))^(1 / cr[["nu"]])
}
at_f <- function(yy) {
  i <- which.min(abs(t_fwd - yy))
  c(rich = richards_ext(t_fwd[i]), harm = ssa_fwd[i])
}
f2050 <- at_f(2050); f2100 <- at_f(2100)
ceiling_rich <- fitA$upper_r
```

Subtracting the fitted Richards curve from the observed anomaly leaves the total harmonic component: everything the secular growth curve does not describe. Its standard deviation is `r sprintf("%.3f", sd_natural)` K, so it is signal and not fitting error, and any statement about the record outside the observation window has to carry it in full rather than in part.


**A model of the harmonic component has to carry the whole of it.** A superposition of fixed-period sinusoids does not: with `r length(per_fix)` periods it recovers `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cov_fix_total)` of the variance of the component and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cov_fix_low)` of the part above two years. The reason is visible in the fitted amplitudes — the eleven-year sinusoid takes only a few hundredths of a degree, far below what the Schwabe band contributes in the SSA decomposition. A single frequency cannot represent a carrier whose amplitude and phase are modulated across the record, which is the same reason a subspace method was used in Section 3.4 rather than a single-frequency regression.

The SSA reconstruction does carry it. With a window of `r L_nat` months and the leading `r R_COMP` eigentriples it reproduces `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cov_total)` of the variance of the component and `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cov_low)` of the part above two years, against a ceiling of `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * frac_low)` set by the fraction of the variance that lies above that cut-off at all — the remainder being month-to-month and interannual noise that no deterministic model should reproduce. The extrapolation is then the linear recurrence of that reconstruction, applied forward and, on the reversed series, backward. The fixed-period synthesis is retained in @fig-natural as a structurally different comparison, and the difference between the two extrapolators is a more honest uncertainty scale than either one's internal error.

**What the longest mode is worth.** The largest single contribution to the component is a mode of roughly `r sprintf("%.0f", mode_tbl$period[which.max(mode_tbl$share)])` yr carrying `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * max(mode_tbl$share))` of its variance. A period of that length is seen about `r sprintf("%.1f", REC_LEN / mode_tbl$period[which.max(mode_tbl$share)])` times in `r sprintf("%.0f", REC_LEN)` yr of data, and the Fourier bins either side of it lie at `r sprintf("%.0f", REC_LEN)` and `r sprintf("%.0f", REC_LEN/3)` yr, so the resolution there is of the order of the estimate itself.

Two checks settle the question and both come out negative. Removing the secular part in structurally different ways moves the leading period from `r sprintf("%.0f", per_range[1])` to `r sprintf("%.0f", per_range[2])` yr (@tbl-detrend): the value is a property of the curve subtracted, not of the SST record, which is what a secular misfit projecting onto the longest available mode looks like. And the solar proxy, over a `r sprintf("%.0f", sol_span)`-yr record that constrains long periods better than the SST does, carries its longest mode at `r sprintf("%.0f", sol_long)` yr. The near-coincidence of the fitted period with the Gleissberg cycle conventionally quoted at 88 yr is therefore not evidence of one. Only the `r sprintf("%.0f", detrend_tbl$period[detrend_tbl$removal == "cubic polynomial"])`-yr mode, which appears under two independent removals, behaves like a property of the record; its length is in the range usually associated with Atlantic multidecadal variability.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-detrend
#| tbl-cap: "Leading SSA period of the harmonic component when the secular part is removed in different ways. A period that changes with the removal is a property of the detrending, not of the record."
detrend_tbl %>%
  transmute(`Secular part removed` = removal,
            `Leading period (yr)` = round(period, 1),
            `Share of variance` = sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * share)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "r", "r"))
```

**Every long period in this analysis is close to a window length in the method.** @tbl-windows puts them side by side. The spacing of the minima in the extrapolated baseline equals the training span because the basis is cyclic on it; the periodogram of the harmonic component peaks at half the record length, which is its second Fourier harmonic and also where a residual secular misfit projects; the leading SSA period under a sigmoid removal sits between the two. None of these is independent evidence of an 88-yr solar cycle, and the agreement among them is a property of a `r sprintf("%.0f", REC_LEN)`-yr record analysed with windows of that order, not a physical result. A genuine test needs either a longer record or a phase comparison across ocean basins, neither of which is attempted here.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-windows
#| tbl-cap: "Long periods reported in this study alongside the method window that could produce each. Agreement between them is expected from the construction and is not evidence of a common physical cycle."
tibble(
  Quantity = c("Spacing of the two minima of the extrapolated baseline (@fig-preind-split)",
               "Span of the GAM training window (cyclic basis period)",
               "Leading SSA period of the harmonic component, Richards removed (@tbl-detrend)",
               "Leading SSA period, LOESS or cubic removed (@tbl-detrend)",
               "Half the record length",
               "Longest mode of the solar proxy over its own record",
               "Gleissberg cycle as conventionally quoted"),
  `Years` = c(trough_gap, train_span,
              detrend_tbl$period[detrend_tbl$removal == "Richards curve"],
              detrend_tbl$period[detrend_tbl$removal == "cubic polynomial"],
              REC_LEN / 2, sol_long, 88)
) %>%
  mutate(Years = round(Years, 1)) %>%
  kable(align = c("l", "r"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-natural
#| fig-cap: "The total harmonic component and its extension outside the record. **A** observed anomaly minus the fitted Richards curve, with the SSA reconstruction and the fixed-period synthesis. **B** backcast to 1600 by the linear recurrence of the reconstruction; the shaded band marks the Maunder Minimum and the Little Ice Age, the dotted line the order of magnitude of the global cooling that proxy reconstructions attribute to it, the dashed curve the fixed-period variant. **C** forward extension to 2100, the harmonic part being the reconstruction inside the record and the recurrent forecast after it. Ribbons are twice the standard deviation of the part of the component the reconstruction does not carry."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 11

pA <- tibble(dt.mnth = time, total = natural, ssa = rec_nat, fixp = fix_in) %>%
  ggplot(aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = total, colour = "total (observed - Richards)"), linewidth = .25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ssa,   colour = "SSA reconstruction"), linewidth = .8) +
  geom_line(aes(y = fixp,  colour = "fixed-period synthesis"), linewidth = .6, linetype = 2) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = .3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("total (observed - Richards)" = "grey72",
                                 "SSA reconstruction"     = "firebrick",
                                 "fixed-period synthesis" = "steelblue4")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (K)", colour = NULL,
       title = "A  Total harmonic component and two models of it",
       subtitle = sprintf("SSA %.0f%% of the variance (%.0f%% above 2 yr); fixed periods %.0f%% (%.0f%%)",
                          100 * cov_total, 100 * cov_low, 100 * cov_fix_total, 100 * cov_fix_low)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

dfB <- bind_rows(
  tibble(dt.mnth = t_bwd, ssa = ssa_bwd, fixp = pred_fix(t_bwd), part = "backcast"),
  tibble(dt.mnth = time,  ssa = rec_nat, fixp = fix_in,          part = "in record"))
pB <- ggplot(dfB, aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  annotate("rect", xmin = LIA[1], xmax = LIA[2], ymin = -Inf, ymax = Inf,
           fill = "steelblue", alpha = .12) +
  geom_ribbon(data = dplyr::filter(dfB, part == "backcast"),
              aes(ymin = ssa - 2 * noise_sd, ymax = ssa + 2 * noise_sd),
              fill = "firebrick", alpha = .12) +
  geom_line(data = dplyr::filter(dfB, part == "backcast"),
            aes(y = fixp), colour = "steelblue4", linewidth = .55, linetype = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ssa, colour = part), linewidth = .7) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, linewidth = .3) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = -0.5, linetype = 3, colour = "darkred") +
  annotate("text", x = 1700, y = -0.45, size = 3,
           label = "global LIA cooling in proxy reconstructions ~ -0.5 K") +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("backcast" = "firebrick", "in record" = "grey45")) +
  coord_cartesian(ylim = c(-0.6, 0.4)) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (K)", colour = NULL,
       title = "B  Backcast of the total harmonic component to 1600",
       subtitle = "shaded: Maunder Minimum / Little Ice Age, 1645-1725") +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

dfC <- bind_rows(
  tibble(dt.mnth = time,  harm = rec_nat, part = "in record"),
  tibble(dt.mnth = t_fwd, harm = ssa_fwd, part = "forecast")) %>%
  mutate(richards = richards_ext(dt.mnth), total = richards + harm) %>%
  dplyr::filter(dt.mnth >= 1980)
pC <- ggplot(dfC, aes(x = dt.mnth)) +
  geom_ribbon(data = dplyr::filter(dfC, part == "forecast"),
              aes(ymin = total - 2 * noise_sd, ymax = total + 2 * noise_sd),
              fill = "firebrick", alpha = .12) +
  geom_line(data = tibble(dt.mnth = time, y = dat$anomaly) %>%
              dplyr::filter(dt.mnth >= 1980),
            aes(y = y, colour = "observed anomaly"), linewidth = .25) +
  geom_line(aes(y = richards, colour = "Richards, extended"), linewidth = 1.1) +
  geom_line(aes(y = total, colour = "Richards + harmonic"), linewidth = .6) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = ceiling_rich, linetype = 3) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = rec_to, linewidth = .3) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = c("observed anomaly" = "grey72",
                                 "Richards, extended" = "darkcyan",
                                 "Richards + harmonic" = "firebrick")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "anomaly (K)", colour = NULL,
       title = "C  Forward extension to 2100, emission conditions unchanged",
       subtitle = sprintf("ceiling %.2f K is extrapolated, not estimated", ceiling_rich)) +
  theme_minimal(base_size = 10)

if (requireNamespace("patchwork", quietly = TRUE)) {
  patchwork::wrap_plots(pA, pB, pC, ncol = 1)
} else { print(pA); print(pB); print(pC) }
```

**The backcast does not produce a Little Ice Age.** Extended to 1600, the harmonic component oscillates between `r sprintf("%+.2f", min(ssa_bwd))` and `r sprintf("%+.2f", max(ssa_bwd))` K, and over 1645–1725 it averages `r sprintf("%+.3f", lia_mean)` K with extremes of `r sprintf("%+.3f", lia_min)` and `r sprintf("%+.3f", lia_max)` K. The fixed-period synthesis, a structurally different extrapolator, stays within `r sprintf("%.2f", max(abs(fix_lia)))` K over the same interval. Proxy reconstructions place the global cooling of the Little Ice Age at a few tenths of a degree, with substantially larger regional excursions — an order of magnitude above what the extrapolated harmonic field delivers, and of no particular sign at those dates. The conclusion does not depend on how much of the component the model carries: it was reached with a model recovering a third of the variance and it survives one recovering `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * cov_total)`.

This is a negative result and it should be reported as one. The oscillatory modes present in the ocean record between `r sprintf("%.0f", rec_from)` and `r sprintf("%.0f", rec_to)` do not, continued backwards, account for the Little Ice Age. That is not evidence against the decomposition: the Maunder Minimum is a multi-century depression of solar activity rather than a phase of any cycle resolvable in a `r sprintf("%.0f", REC_LEN)`-year window, and the coldest decades of the period coincide with a dense sequence of large tropical eruptions, a forcing this analysis contains no term for. The proper reading is that the harmonic component estimated here describes the decadal-to-multidecadal variability of the instrumental era and carries no information about century-scale forcing. A backcast that *had* reproduced the Little Ice Age from eleven- and twenty-two-year modes would have been a reason for suspicion, not for confidence.

**The forward extension states an assumption, not a projection.** Adding the extended Richards curve to the recurrent forecast of the harmonic component gives `r sprintf("%+.2f", f2050[["rich"]] + f2050[["harm"]])` K in 2050 and `r sprintf("%+.2f", f2100[["rich"]] + f2100[["harm"]])` K in 2100, approaching the fitted ceiling of `r sprintf("%.2f", ceiling_rich)` K. Three cautions attach to that number and none of them is small. The record covers only `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * span_reached)` of the fitted sigmoid, so the ceiling is set by the functional form rather than by the data. The saturation of a Richards curve is an empirical shape with no emission term in it: the curve cannot represent a change in emissions, and reading it as "what happens if CO$_2$ forcing continues as it has" imports an assumption the fit never tested. And a recurrent forecast reproduces the modes of the observation window, so its skill decays with horizon in a way the ribbon in @fig-natural does not show. The honest statement is conditional and bounded: *if* the secular component continues along the shape fitted to `r sprintf("%.0f", rec_from)`–`r sprintf("%.0f", rec_to)`, the ocean surface approaches `r sprintf("%.2f", ceiling_rich)` K above the record mean, with decadal excursions of the order of `r sprintf("%.2f", 2 * noise_sd)` K about it. Tying that to a Keeling-curve scenario requires a forcing term in the model, which is the natural next step and is not attempted here.

## Location parameter versus inflection

In the Richards parametrisation used here, $t_0$ enters as a location parameter inside a power-transformed logistic kernel; the date of maximum acceleration follows from $\mathrm{d}^2y/\mathrm{d}t^2 = 0$, which gives $e^{-B(t-t_0)} = \nu$ and hence $t_{\mathrm{infl}} = t_0 - \ln\nu/B$, which coincides with $t_0$ only for $\nu = 1$. `r growth_discussion`

### Identifiability of the growth-curve step {#sec-growth-identifiability}

Whether an inflection exists at all is a property of the baseline, not of the observations alone, and the two candidate bases differ in exactly the way that matters.

A non-cyclic basis continues approximately linearly beyond its training range, so the extrapolated baseline after `r SPLIT_YEAR` is a straight line and the residual against it retains whatever curvature the observations have — which, over `r SPLIT_YEAR`–`r sprintf("%.0f", rec_to)`, is close to monotone acceleration with no flattening. A sigmoid fitted to such a residual has no information about its upper asymptote; the likelihood is flat along the ridge that trades asymptote against rate, and the optimiser returns a near-zero rate with the inflection at the edge of the search range. That is precisely what @tbl-basis shows for both `cr` variants.

The cyclic basis used here behaves differently. It forces the fitted function to return to its starting value and slope at the end of the training window, so the extrapolation oscillates about the pre-industrial level rather than continuing upward. Subtracting an oscillating baseline from a rising record produces a residual that flattens towards the end of the record, the upper asymptote becomes estimable from data rather than assumed, and the staged estimator returns a turning point of `r sprintf("%.1f", t_turn_log)` yr that is stable across the two flexibilities tested (@tbl-basis).


The turning point is therefore real given the baseline, and conditional on it. The claim this study can defend is not "the anthropogenic signal turned in `r sprintf("%.0f", t_turn_rich)`" but "if the natural baseline continues quasi-periodically rather than carrying a secular trend of its own, the residual anthropogenic signal turns in `r sprintf("%.0f", t_turn_rich)`". Stating the conditional explicitly is the difference between a result a referee can check and one they will reject. The alternative assumption — a natural baseline with its own secular slope — yields no identifiable turning point at all, and that asymmetry between the two hypotheses should be reported rather than hidden.

## What the mean-cycle control establishes

Replacing the observed solar minima by a regular sequence at the mean cycle length of `r sprintf("%.2f", mean_cycle)` yr removes all information about the timing of individual cycles while preserving the number and average spacing of the spline knots. The band structure of @tbl-esprit survives that substitution, with a maximum period difference of `r sprintf("%.2f", max_dT)` yr, and the non-harmonic trend changes by an RMS of only `r sprintf("%.3f", rmse_constructions)` °C.

Two conclusions follow. The modes are properties of the SST record rather than consequences of the anchoring, which answers the circularity objection directly. And the construction spread provides an uncertainty scale for the reported periods that does not depend on an independence assumption the residuals violate — a more defensible bound, in this setting, than a nominal standard error.

## Relation to index-regression approaches

Methods that regress temperature on ENSO, volcanic and solar indices (Foster and Rahmstorf 2011) and the present decomposition answer complementary questions. Index regression asks how much variance a prescribed set of predictors explains; the present approach asks what oscillatory structure the record itself contains once a physically anchored trend has been removed, and estimates the periods and stationarity of that structure rather than assuming them. The agreement of the ESPRIT periods with the canonical Schwabe, Hale and recharge-oscillator bands is therefore a consistency check on the construction, not a result imported from the predictors.

## Limitations

**The ceiling is not estimated.** The record covers `r sprintf("%.0f%%", 100 * span_reached)` of the fitted sigmoid, so the upper asymptote of `r sprintf("%.2f", upper_asymptote.rich)` °C in @tbl-turning is determined by the functional form and not by the observations. The turning point is close to the end of the window and is the quantity the data constrain; the asymptote should be read as what the fitted curve implies, not as a projection of ocean warming.

**Extrapolation of the alternative baseline.** The GAM route of Section 3.6, retained for comparison in @tbl-aic, defines its residual against a model fitted to `r sprintf("%.0f", rec_from)`–`r SPLIT_YEAR` and evaluated to `r sprintf("%.0f", rec_to)` — over a range where the smoother is unconstrained by data. The cyclic basis makes that extrapolation quasi-periodic by construction: the baseline after `r SPLIT_YEAR` repeats the pre-industrial pattern because the basis requires it to, not because the ocean was observed to do so. @tbl-basis bounds what the choice costs. The solar-locked route avoids the extrapolation entirely — its trend is anchored to solar phase over the whole record — which is the main reason it is used for the headline figures.

**Choice of split year.** `r SPLIT_YEAR` is imposed as a calendar boundary on the argument that industrial influence on SST was negligible before it. An independent rolling-correlation analysis in this project placed the pre-industrial/modern boundary near late 1987. The decomposition should be repeated across a range of split years and the sensitivity of $t_0$, $\nu$ and the trough amplitudes reported as a curve rather than a single value.

**Nature of the reported intervals.** The intervals in @tbl-turning are model-conditional and assume independent residuals. The residuals of a monthly SST series are strongly autocorrelated, so the effective sample size is far below `r N` and these intervals are optimistic. A moving-block bootstrap over the residual series is the appropriate replacement.

**Attribution language.** The residual against a natural baseline is not by itself an anthropogenic signal; it is everything the baseline model does not capture, including volcanic forcing, aerosol effects and any residual instrumental inhomogeneity. The term "industrial component" is used in that operational sense throughout.

**Resolution limits.** The bidecadal mode is sampled only about `r sprintf("%.0f", (rec_to - rec_from)/T12)` times in the record, so its damping rate is weakly constrained and its near-unit modulus should be read as consistent with stationarity rather than as evidence for it.

# Conclusions

1.  Anchoring a cubic spline to the minima of the solar power variation isolates a solar-locked trend whose non-harmonic part has minima near `r sprintf("%.0f", Min_early)` and `r sprintf("%.0f", Min_mid)` and a turning point near `r sprintf("%.0f", Turn_late)`.
2.  SSA with ESPRIT resolves the detrended field into a near-stationary bidecadal mode at `r sprintf("%.1f", T12)` yr, a split Schwabe band at `r sprintf("%.1f", T34)` and `r sprintf("%.1f", T56)` yr indicating amplitude and phase modulation, and an interannual band at `r sprintf("%.1f", T910)`–`r sprintf("%.1f", T78)` yr.
3.  A mean-cycle control, with knots at the regular interval of `r sprintf("%.2f", mean_cycle)` yr, reproduces the same band structure to within `r sprintf("%.2f", max_dT)` yr. The oscillatory modes are therefore properties of the SST record and not artefacts of phase-accurate knot placement.
4.  Defining the industrial component as the residual against a cyclic GAM baseline trained on the pre-`r SPLIT_YEAR` record yields `r growth_conclusion`. The estimate is conditional on that basis: a non-cyclic baseline identifies no turning point (@tbl-basis).
5.  The sensitivity of that step to the extrapolation basis (@tbl-basis) is larger than any other uncertainty in the study, and is the first thing a referee should be shown rather than the last.
6.  Natural multi-decadal minima near `r sprintf("%.0f", trough_early$dt.mnth)` and `r sprintf("%.0f", trough_late$dt.mnth)` oppose the industrial trend, so trends fitted to the raw record over the late twentieth century understate the underlying forced rate. The magnitude of this effect depends on the extrapolated baseline and is bounded by the sensitivities in Section 5.5.
